content.p: Shortly after 4 a.m. on 5 September 1972, eight men in tracksuits climbed a fence into the Olympic Village in Munich, carrying sports bags. Within minutes they were inside the apartments of the Israeli team. By the early hours of the next morning, eleven Israeli coaches and athletes were dead, along with a West German police officer, and a rescue operation that had been planned by the host nation had collapsed into a night-time firefight on an air base outside the city.

The attackers belonged to Black September, a Palestinian militant group. They demanded the release of prisoners in Israel and in West Germany. Germany, which had wanted to use its first Olympic Games since Berlin in 1936 to present a relaxed and peaceful face, was left to deal with the crisis on its own soil. How it did so, and how it treated the victims' families for fifty years afterwards, became a story of its own that was only formally acknowledged in 2022.

The 1972 Games, which opened on 26 August, were billed as the "Games of Joy". According to the Los Angeles Times, the idea was to show how much the country had changed since 1945. HISTORY reports that West Germany chose unarmed guards over uniformed soldiers and police to keep the atmosphere light. The Los Angeles Times adds that about 2,000 "security officers" in light-blue uniforms patrolled the Olympic Park, equipped with walkie-talkies rather than guns, and that none of them were stationed at the village.

Israel sent its largest delegation to date. According to HISTORY, citing the book One Day in September by Simon Reeve, several of the older members still carried the physical and mental scars of Nazi concentration camps. HISTORY also reports that Israeli officials had voiced concern about the lack of security and that a New York Times report in 1972 described "glaring" deficiencies.

On the night of 4 September, the Los Angeles Times says, much of the team went to a German-language performance of Fiddler on the Roof. Coach Amitzur Shapira, whose sprinter Esther Shakhamorov Roth had just advanced in the hurdles, translated for her in Yiddish. After midnight the delegation returned to the village.

The Los Angeles Times describes a chain-link fence about six and a half feet high with no barbed wire. Near Gate 25A, which was locked at midnight but left unguarded, the men in sweatsuits bearing the names of Arab countries reached the fence at the same moment as a group of American athletes returning from a night out. By that newspaper's account, one of the men was helped over by an American, and officials who saw them, including German postmen, took them for ordinary athletes. HISTORY likewise says the group was helped over a wire fence by athletes who mistook them for fellow competitors.

Of the 28 Israeli delegation members, 21, all men, lived at 31 Connollystrasse. The attackers entered Apartment 1 with a key. Wrestling referee Yossef Gutfreund, 40, heard it scrape in the lock, saw gun barrels in the dim light, shouted a warning and threw his weight against the door. A roommate, wrestling coach Tuvia Sokolovsky, smashed a window and escaped. The Los Angeles Times adds that the attackers passed over Apartment 2, where five other Israelis, among them the race walker Shaul Ladany, were sleeping.

In another room, Moshe Weinberg, a 33-year-old wrestling coach, went for the leader with a fruit knife, and a shot tore through his cheek. In Apartment 3 the attackers rounded up weightlifters David Berger, Ze'ev Friedman and Yossef Romano, and wrestlers Eliezer Halfin and Mark Slavin, the last of whom was 18 and had arrived in Israel only four months earlier. A wrestler who had finished competing, Gad Tsobari, opened his door to see what the noise was. Led out at gunpoint, he pushed a rifle aside and ran through the underground car park, past shots, until he reached the press centre.

The accounts of the first deaths differ slightly. The National Park Service, citing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, says Romano grabbed an attacker's gun and was shot, and that Weinberg was killed while trying to attack a kidnapper as the hostages were moved. The Los Angeles Times says Weinberg punched and tackled one of the attackers during the move and was shot in the chest, and that Romano died in Apartment 1, where the other nine spent most of their remaining hours with his body on the floor in front of them. Weinberg's body was later thrown into the street.

The first call to the Munich police, from a cleaner who had heard shots, came at 4:47 a.m., according to the Los Angeles Times. At about 5:10 a typed communique was dropped from a window. The Los Angeles Times reports that it demanded the release of 234 prisoners in Israeli jails and of two in Germany, the radicals Andreas Baader and Ulrike Meinhof, with a 9 a.m. deadline. The BBC's timeline puts the Israeli figure at 236. The nine hostages were Gutfreund, Berger, Friedman, Halfin, Shapira, Slavin, Kehat Shorr, Andre Spitzer and Yakov Springer (spelled Shpringer in the Los Angeles Times).

Israel's government gave its answer quickly. Prime Minister Golda Meir was quoted by HISTORY as saying that if Israel gave in, "no Israeli anywhere in the world can feel that his life is safe." The negotiating was left to the Germans. According to the National Park Service, Munich's police chief and the head of the Egyptian Olympic team offered the attackers unlimited money, and the Tunisian and Libyan ambassadors to Germany also tried to mediate, all without result. The deadline was extended several times.

The Los Angeles Times lays the lack of preparation bare: Germany had no on-call tactical unit, and a late-afternoon plan to storm the building was abandoned when police realised that the world, and probably the attackers, were watching live television of officers disguised in tracksuits creeping across the roof. The hooded figure on the balcony became the day's defining image. HISTORY reports that more than 900 million people watched coverage of the attack, and that it was the first act of terror to be broadcast live during a major sporting event.

Inside the building, Spitzer was brought to a window at about 5 p.m. and struck with a gun butt after speaking briefly to officials below. Walther Troger, the head of the Olympic village, and Interior Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher were allowed in and saw nine living hostages and Romano's body. Troger later described the mood in the room as "not very hopeful".

The Los Angeles Times also describes photographs it obtained of Romano's body and says they strongly suggest he was mutilated, although it adds that such evidence is not definitive. Citing the book One Day in September, it quotes Jamal Al-Gashey, who survived the night, as calling any suggestion that Romano was tortured a "complete lie", while Romano's widow, Ilana, and Spitzer's widow, Ankie, are convinced he was.

The Olympics themselves carried on for most of the day. AFP records that the Games were halted at 3:50 p.m. local time, for 34 hours, "a first in Olympic history". The Los Angeles Times says the executive board of the International Olympic Committee, whose outgoing president Avery Brundage wanted the crisis resolved, had recorded that "the Games must continue at all costs", and that a memorial service and a resumption of events were already pencilled in for the next day.

Around 10 p.m. the attackers' demand for transport to Cairo was met on paper. According to the Los Angeles Times, the Germans told them the request had been accepted while preparing an ambush at the military airfield at Fürstenfeldbruck, about 14 miles west of Munich. Two helicopters flew the eight attackers and nine hostages there.

That plan was undermined from the start. The Los Angeles Times, citing German after-action reports summarised in legal documents filed in a Bavarian court, lists the problems. Police were working on the assumption that there were five attackers, not eight, and nobody told the five riflemen at the airfield in time. They were not specially trained marksmen, had no body armour, steel helmets or night scopes, and had no radios to talk to one another. Armored cars were delayed by a traffic jam of onlookers heading for the airfield. The National Park Service reaches a similar verdict, calling the operation a fiasco.

The most serious failure involved the Lufthansa Boeing 727 that stood on the apron as the supposed escape aircraft. A team of 17 armed police officers had been placed aboard to overpower the first attackers to inspect it. The Los Angeles Times says the officers judged the position suicidal, because a single grenade would be lethal in the confined space and the plane held nearly 10,000 gallons of fuel, and left before the helicopters landed. The National Park Service describes the same abandonment.

The order to fire came shortly after the helicopters landed at about 10:40 p.m. The Los Angeles Times says only two snipers fired, wasting the chance to hit as many attackers as possible with the first volley. A gunbattle of more than an hour followed. The control-tower officer Anton Fliegerbauer was killed. Just after midnight, according to the National Park Service, attackers fired into the helicopters, and a grenade was thrown into one of them. The Los Angeles Times says that Berger was hit in the thigh by a bullet, but, according to an autopsy report cited in legal papers, died from smoke inhalation.

Five attackers were killed, among them the group's leader, known as Issa (Luttif Afif). Three were captured. The Spyscape article gives a different count, four, in its account of the night; most of the other sources opened for this account, including HISTORY, the BBC, The Guardian and the Associated Press, say five.

Through the evening, news agencies reported that the hostages had been saved. According to AFP, government spokesman Conrad Ahlers announced a successful rescue toward midnight. The agency's reporter Charles Bietry, doubting it, stayed at the scene and saw the mayor of Munich, Georg Kronawitter, emerge in tears saying that everything had gone wrong and all the hostages were dead. AFP's flash that "all the hostages have been killed" went out at 2:16 a.m., and German authorities confirmed it 56 minutes later. Bietry later recalled that the radio carried celebrations from Israel, where people believed the hostages were safe. On ABC, Jim McKay told American viewers: "Our worst fears have been realized tonight." The Israeli delegation chief, Shmuel Lalkin, identified the bodies; he later said he brought home ten coffins.

The International Olympic Committee decided on the morning of 6 September that the Games should go on. Brundage said the public would agree that "a handful of terrorists" should not be allowed to destroy the nucleus of international goodwill. HISTORY says a memorial service in the Olympic Stadium was attended by 3,000 athletes and 80,000 spectators, and that the remaining Israeli team members left Munich, as did Mark Spitz and several other teams.

The three surviving attackers did not stay in custody for long. On 29 October 1972, The Guardian reported, a Lufthansa airliner flying from Damascus to Frankfurt was hijacked after leaving Beirut, with only 11 male passengers on board, and forced to land in Munich. Chancellor Willy Brandt gave in within hours and handed over the three men. Israel had not been consulted. HISTORY says they were given a hero's welcome in Libya.

The Guardian's article, based on the documentary One Day in September, says Al-Gashey alleged that the hijacking had been agreed with the German government in advance, and that Brandt denied any deal. The paper says Al-Gashey's account was supported by a range of senior German, Palestinian and Israeli sources, among them Ulrich Wegener, a key aide of the interior minister who founded the GSG-9 counter-terrorism unit. Wegener said that Bonn did not want to risk further confrontation with Palestinian groups. Ankie Spitzer told the paper she blamed the terrorists, but "most of all" the German authorities.

The Guardian says Meir authorised the Mossad to begin Operation Wrath of God within hours of hearing of the release; Al-Monitor's report from AFP gives the historian Michael Bar-Zohar's account that Meir, her Mossad chief Zvi Zamir and her counter-terrorism adviser Aharon Yariv decided on a strategy of killing the leadership of Black September, and that Meir hesitated before authorising it. Spyscape describes a body called Committee X, which Meir formed with Defense Minister Moshe Dayan and two other ministers to consider whom to target on Mossad's recommendation, as former prime minister Ehud Barak told a documentary series.

Spyscape lists the Fatah spokesman Wael Zuaiter, as the first target, shot dead in Rome on 16 October 1972, and Mahmoud Hamshari, the PLO representative in Paris, two months later. Barak told AFP that in April 1973 he took part, dressed as a woman, in a raid in Beirut in which three Palestinians were killed, along with two Israelis and several Lebanese civilians.

In July 1973 the campaign went wrong. In the Norwegian town of Lillehammer, Israeli agents shot a Moroccan waiter, Ahmed Bouchikhi (spelt Bouchiki by Spyscape), who was not the Black September commander Ali Hassan Salameh they were hunting. The two accounts of the aftermath differ on numbers: AFP says three Israeli agents were arrested and spent 22 months in prison, while Spyscape names five who were convicted and later pardoned. In 1996 Israel paid undisclosed compensation to Bouchikhi's family without admitting responsibility, and a Norwegian commission said in 2000 that the killing was a violation of Norwegian sovereignty. Salameh himself was killed by a car bomb in Beirut in January 1979, according to AFP and HISTORY.

The families spent decades seeking an apology, access to official files and greater compensation. Immediately after the attack, Germany made payments to relatives of about 4.19 million marks, according to Germany's interior ministry, and in 2002 they received a further 3 million euros, according to the dpa news agency, both as reported by the Associated Press. Before the 50th anniversary, JNS reports, an offer of 4.5 million euros was on the table; AP says the initial offer was 10 million euros, and JNS reports that the families warned they would boycott the commemoration if the offer stood.

On 31 August 2022 Germany agreed on a total of 28 million euros, including the earlier payments, JNS and AP report. It also agreed to acknowledge the failures of the authorities and to let German and Israeli historians review the events. Speaking beside Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, at the anniversary ceremony, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier called it "shameful" that the agreement had taken 50 years and said Germany had for too long refused to accept its share of responsibility for the athletes' safety.

The eight-member international commission began its three-year work on 30 May 2023, with the interior ministry promising to examine the period before and after the attack and the treatment of the families.

Remembrance inside the Olympic movement came slowly. At the Athens ceremony in 2004, the BBC reported, IOC president Jacques Rogge attended the annual service, which relatives said was the first time a sitting IOC president had done so, and said the killings had "forever changed the relationship between sport and politics"; the widows of Romano and Spitzer were still asking for an official mention at opening ceremonies.
